title: POC Benchmark Blueprint: load modeling, streaming vs batch
next_steps: Redwood to share benchmark harness template and example customer script (Maria) - target 2025-08-08
Customer to provide representative prompt set + token distribution (Priya) - target 2025-08-11
SE-led baseline run on Redwood hosted model (Diego) - target 2025-08-15
Follow-up deep-dive to review baseline results and determine Dedicated sizing (30-45m) - schedule week of 2025-08-18
action_items: Maria Chen - Share harness repo link and README - 2025-08-08
Priya Shah - Upload 3 sample workloads (chat transcripts, summarization, search-rerank) - 2025-08-11
Diego Alvarez - Configure baseline harness and run 1x non-streaming and 1x streaming run - 2025-08-15
Tom Reynolds - Provide target p95 latency and max acceptable cost per 1k tokens - 2025-08-11
Renee Park - Draft initial Dedicated sizing recommendation after baseline - 2025-08-19
summary: POC scoping focused on planning benchmark runs and integrating Clearwave's customer scripts into Redwood's harness. Team aligned on success criteria (p95 latency, throughput, and quality fidelity vs. current on-prem model), discussed streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs for chat workloads, defined minimal dataset to iterate quickly, and set an aggressive two-week baseline timeline. Security and data handling caveats noted (no PHI in sample sets; use synthetic data or hashed IDs).
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-05
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maria Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Renee Park (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Clearwave Head of ML), Tom Reynolds (Clearwave SRE), Aisha Mohamed (Product), Liam O'Neill (Eng), Jared (Intern)

[00:00] Maria Chen: All right everyone, thanks for joining. Quick agenda — scope the benchmark, decide what scripts and workloads you can give us, streaming vs non-streaming approach, and agree on success criteria. If we can get that, we'll run a baseline within two weeks.

[00:24] Priya Shah: Thanks Maria. To start, our main goal is to validate latency at scale and make sure outputs match our current on-prem model for clinical summarization. We also need to understand cost tradeoffs — we can't exceed x dollars per 1k tokens for the POC.

[00:45] Diego Alvarez: Great. Can you give us rough QPS and concurrency numbers? If not exact, a typical peak for the POC is fine.

[00:52] Priya Shah: Peak concurrent sessions probably 120, average QPS ~18, bursts up to 35 for a few minutes. Typical prompt length for summarization is 800-1,200 tokens input, outputs 150-400 tokens. For the chat product we have many short prompts, 40-200 tokens.

[01:18] Tom Reynolds: On the infra side we care about p95 under a 120-concurrency load and how the model behaves when KV cache warmup is happening. Also, we want to check graceful fallback if dedicated capacity is saturated.

[01:34] Diego Alvarez: Noted. For the harness integration: we can take your existing scripts — Python-based runner with a simple JSON per-call format — and drop them into our harness. Two integration modes: non-streaming (complete request/response) and streaming (token-by-token / chunked). Streaming has different metrics (first-byte latency, tail latency, and throughput of token/s).

[02:06] Priya Shah: Is there a big difference in cost between streaming and non-streaming? Our initial intuition was streaming is more efficient for long outputs but adds complexity.

[02:16] Renee Park: It depends. Streaming can reduce perceived latency for users because they see tokens earlier, but for batching and GPU utilization, streaming can increase overhead if you do tiny token flushes. Our optimize toolkit can suggest batching + mini-aggregation to balance cost and first-byte latency.

[02:38] Aisha Mohamed: For the POC success criteria, we have product-level metrics: p95 under 800ms for short-chat, p95 under 3s for summarization, and quality parity for the top-3 metrics in your eval (ROUGE/semantic similarity). Also uptime during test windows must be >99.5%.

[03:02] Maria Chen: Helpful. We'll codify success criteria into the harness so pass/fail is automated: latency checks, token-per-second throughput, and sample-based quality checks (we'll compute embeddings similarity vs your reference outputs).

[03:19] Priya Shah: About data — our engineers will scrub PHI and supply synthetic IDs. We won't send real patient data. Can Redwood confirm that the hosted baseline run will not persist payloads beyond logs and will follow our data-retention spec?

[03:36] Maria Chen: Yes, for the hosted baseline we use ephemeral storage for calls; logs are retained per your retention window. We'll share our data handling doc after the call. Also, if you prefer, we can run the same harness against a Private (VPC) node later.

[03:52] Liam O'Neill: One technical question: our current model uses KV cache warmstart across sessions to speed up repeated prompts. Can we replicate that in the harness?

[04:03] Diego Alvarez: We support prefix caching and KV simulation in the harness. For the benchmark, we can run a warm cache scenario and a cold cache scenario. We'll need samples that show repeated tokens so cache hits are realistic.

[04:21] Tom Reynolds: On monitoring, we want token-level cost breakdowns and per-route latency. Is that available in the baseline reports?

[04:29] Renee Park: Yes, baseline report will include per-route token counts, cost estimate, p50/p95/p99 latencies, GPU utilization, and error rates. We'll push a CSV and a dashboard snapshot to your shared folder.

[04:44] Priya Shah: For scripts, our team currently has a mix: a Go-based load generator for concurrency, plus Python unit scripts that call our local serving layer. Is that an integration problem?

[04:58] Diego Alvarez: Not at all. The harness supports a simple HTTP client wrapper. We prefer Python for the orchestration pieces but we can run remote Go clients or ask your team to wrap Go calls into the JSON format. We'll share an example runner.

[05:13] Maria Chen: Let's outline the benchmark matrix. Suggested runs:
- Baseline (non-streaming) at 1x workload profile (target QPS, cold cache)
- Baseline (non-streaming) warm cache
- Streaming run (simulate token streaming with client flush every 50 tokens)
- Stress test (2x peak) to check graceful degradation and fallbacks
- Quality evaluation run (sample 200 calls and compute similarity)

[05:52] Priya Shah: That looks reasonable. For the streaming run, do you simulate partial token batching on the server or does the client dictate chunking?

[06:03] Renee Park: The client chunk size informs the server behavior; however, our runtime can coalesce streaming token pieces within a short window to make batching effective. There's a knob for max stream flush interval. We'll record both first-byte and final-token latencies.

[06:22] Jared: Quick naive question — when you say coalesce, does that add jitter?

[06:27] Diego Alvarez: It can add a few ms of jitter for the first tokens but overall reduces GPU idle time and cost. It's a tradeoff. We'll show both extremes in the results so you can pick what matches product UX.

[06:40] Tom Reynolds: Can Redwood simulate connection drops during streaming so we can check resume/fallback behavior?

[06:47] Maria Chen: Yes we can simulate network flakiness and test the client-side reconnection patterns. We'll coordinate with your SRE to decide realistic drop rates.

[06:58] Priya Shah: How long will each run take? We need to plan testing windows.

[07:03] Diego Alvarez: Typical baseline runs to get statistically meaningful latency percentiles: at least 15-20 minutes at target load per scenario. Stress tests longer, 30-45 minutes. Quality evaluation depends on sample size — 200 samples is quick. Whole matrix in parallel we estimate 6-8 hours of total runtime but we can stage over a few days. For hosted baseline we can kick off everything in one day outside business hours.

[07:36] Aisha Mohamed: Timeline? You said two weeks to baseline earlier. Can you break down tasks?

[07:42] Maria Chen: Sure. Week 1 (this week): Share harness, customer provides scripts and sample sets, Redwood engineers map and set up runs. Week 2: Execute baseline runs, deliver baseline report and a follow-up call to review. If you want Dedicated sizing and private run, that would be an extra week after baseline.

[08:02] Priya Shah: Sounds good. About success criteria again, product wants a hard pass/fail on latency and quality. If we don't hit pass, we pivot to Dedicated sizing tests?

[08:12] Maria Chen: Exactly. If hosted can't meet the SLOs at acceptable cost, we provision a Dedicated pool and re-run the baseline to show delta. We'll also run quantized model variants if you want to explore cost reductions.

[08:27] Priya Shah: We're interested in 4-bit quantization experiments but we need to understand quality implications. Can Redwood provide recommended quant profiles?

[08:36] Renee Park: Yes, after the baseline we'll propose quantization tradeoffs and candidate model variants with measured ROUGE/sem-sim impacts. We keep the eval harness consistent so you can compare apples-to-apples.

[08:47] Liam O'Neill: Small nit: our current orchestration opens about 350 concurrent sockets per worker during peaks. Will that affect the harness?

[08:55] Diego Alvarez: We can throttle client concurrency at the harness level. If you want, we can mirror your socket distribution to test realistic connection counts. Please provide a simple histogram of connection counts per worker.

[09:09] Tom Reynolds: Security: we'll need SOC 2 and encryption at rest details before sending sample scripts from our CI. Also SSO for the console is a must.

[09:21] Maria Chen: We'll attach the SOC 2 summary and our security one-pager after this call. SSO/SAML can be configured; for the POC we'll give you temporary access tokens and audit logs.

[09:32] Priya Shah: One last detail — our acceptance criteria includes cost per 1k tokens. We'll share our internal target range; Redwood should compute a projected cost for the run.

[09:42] Renee Park: We'll include an estimated cost column in the baseline CSV: raw token cost + infra amortized estimate. That estimate will have assumptions spelled out.

[09:52] Maria Chen: Quick recap of action items: Maria shares harness and README; Priya shares three workloads; Diego configures baseline and runs warm/cold and streaming; Renee prepares dashboard template; Tom shares retention/SOC constraints. Then meet to review results.

[10:14] Priya Shah: Ok thanks, folks. Who should I ping if we hit a blocker prepping the scripts?

[10:20] Maria Chen: Ping me or Diego on Slack; Renee for the dashboard. We'll have a Slack channel and share the harness repo link.

[10:28] Aisha Mohamed: Can we also get a short runbook for how to interpret the CSV so Product can read it without engineering?

[10:35] Renee Park: Yup we'll add a README and a quick one-pager that explains p50/p95/p99 columns, cost calc, and a short glossary of streaming vs non-streaming metrics.

[10:44] Priya Shah: Great. That covers my questions. Thanks everyone.

[10:49] Maria Chen: Perfect. We'll follow up with the repo link and security docs by Friday. Meeting adjourn.

End transcript.

Notes on transcript quality: Several acronyms were auto-transcribed weirdly (KV became "K-V", Redwood Dedicated became "Redwood Delicate" in a spot); speaker labels are accurate for Redwood attendees but customer intern was sometimes labeled as Jared only. Minor filler words and overlaps preserved.
notes: Customer emphasized no real PHI in sample datasets - use synthetic or hashed IDs
Redwood will provide both streaming and non-streaming harness examples; streaming will include a flush interval knob
Baseline runs: 15-20min per scenario; stress test 30-45min
Quality eval: 200 samples for quick check; full eval can be larger later
If hosted doesn't meet SLO/cost, plan to test Dedicated and quantized variants
